title: Finance: Financial Documents, Tariffs and Budgets
summary: Reading municipal accounts and statements, checking calculations on financial documents, comparing tariff options, and drawing up and analysing household budgets and income-and-expenditure statements.

notes.text: In the exam you will be given real-looking documents, such as a municipal account, bank statement, payslip, till slip, invoice or cellphone bill, and asked to **read values**, **check calculations** and **make decisions**. Always identify what each column means before you calculate.

notes.caption: Extract from a municipal account for March

notes.title: Worked example 1: completing the account
notes.problem: Calculate the missing values A, B and C on the municipal account.
steps: A (rates): R960 000 × 0,0105 = R10 080 per year; ÷ 12 = R840,00 per month
C (total due): the balance and payment cancel out (R0,00)

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Property rates are usually given as a rate **per rand of valuation per year** (e.g. 0,0105 means about one cent per rand). Divide by 12 for the monthly amount. Some municipalities first subtract a **rebate** (e.g. the first R200 000 of the value) before calculating rates.

notes.title: Worked example 2: two cellphone options
notes.problem: Option A: R199 per month including 2 GB of data, then R89 per extra GB. Option B: R329 per month for 5 GB, then R59 per extra GB. Which is cheaper for 4 GB, and which for 6 GB?
steps: 4 GB, A: R199 + 2 × R89 = R377. B: R329 (within its 5 GB).
notes.answer: Option B is cheaper for both 4 GB (R329 vs R377) and 6 GB (R388 vs R555). Option A is cheaper only for low usage (under about 3,5 GB).

notes.text: A **plan** of expected income and expenditure for a future period (e.g. next month).
A **record** of the actual income and expenditure for a period that has already happened.

items: **Fixed expenses** stay the same each month: rent or bond, insurance, school fees, car instalment.
**Variable expenses** change: groceries, electricity, transport, entertainment.
**Occasional expenses** happen now and then: school uniforms, car service, gifts. Budget for them by saving a little each month.

notes.caption: The Dlamini household's budget and actual spending for July

notes.title: Worked example 3: analysing a budget
notes.problem: (a) Did the Dlaminis have a surplus or deficit in July? (b) What percentage over budget were they on groceries? (c) Comment on their savings.
steps: (a) Income R28 400 − actual spending R28 146 = R254, a small surplus.
(c) They saved nothing although they planned R1 700. The overspending on groceries, petrol and data used up the savings.
notes.answer: (a) Surplus of R254 (b) about 13,1% (c) Overspending on variable expenses meant the planned savings were not made; they should cut back or adjust the budget.

notes.label: Inflation and budgets
notes.text: To plan next year's budget, increase each expense by the expected **inflation rate** (or the item's own rate, e.g. electricity often rises faster). Next year's cost = this year's cost × (1 + inflation rate).

questions.prompt: Which document records what was actually earned and spent last month?
Which of these is usually a fixed monthly expense?
A household has a deficit when its expenditure is greater than its income.
A property is valued at R1 450 000. Rates are charged at 0,0098 per rand per year. Calculate the monthly rates. Give your answer correct to the nearest cent.
The same municipality first subtracts a rebate of R250 000 from the valuation. Calculate the new monthly rates on the R1 450 000 property (0,0098 per rand per year), correct to the nearest cent.
Use the electricity tariff in the notes (R2,74 per kWh for the first 350 kWh, then R3,21). Calculate the cost of 520 kWh.
A family spends R6 800 a month on groceries. Food inflation is expected to be 6,5%. How much should they budget per month for groceries next year?
A household budgeted R3 600 for petrol but spent R4 110. By what percentage did they overspend? Round to one decimal place.
Match each term to its meaning.

questions.prompt: The Dlaminis want to make sure they save R1 700 next month. Use the budget table to suggest THREE realistic changes, and justify each with figures.
questions.memo:
Any three, each with a figure (2 marks each):
✓ groceries: overspent by R815; buy in bulk, compare prices, plan meals to stay within R6 200
✓ transport: overspent by R510; lift club, combine trips or use public transport
✓ cellphones: overspent by R144; buy data bundles instead of out-of-bundle data, use Wi-Fi
✓ pay savings first by debit order on payday so the R1 700 is saved before spending
✓ adjust the budget to realistic amounts and cut a non-essential item
